hook.text: You know what 'dog' means—but can you define meaning itself? It's surprisingly slippery.

buildup.text: Semantics is the branch of linguistics devoted to studying meaning in language.

discovery.text: It asks: how do words, phrases, and sentences carry information from speaker to listener?

twist.text: Meaning isn't just in the dictionary—context, tone, and shared knowledge all contribute.

climax.text: Semantics draws on philosophy, psychology, and logic to crack the code of meaning.

punchline.text: Meaning is everywhere—and nowhere easy to pin down.

hook.text: 'The morning star' and 'the evening star' both refer to Venus—but they mean different things.

buildup.text: Reference is what a word points to in the world; sense is the concept it evokes.

discovery.text: Frege introduced this distinction in 1892—it's still foundational in semantics.

twist.text: Fictional names like 'Sherlock Holmes' have sense but no real-world reference at all.

climax.text: Sense and reference are both part of meaning—but they operate on different planes.

punchline.text: Same target, different lens—that's the sense/reference split.

hook.text: 'Cheap' and 'affordable' denote the same thing—low cost—but they feel completely different.

buildup.text: Denotation is a word's core dictionary meaning; connotation is its emotional coloring.

discovery.text: Advertisers exploit connotation: 'pre-owned' sounds better than 'used,' though both mean the same.

twist.text: Connotations shift across cultures—'blue' signals sadness in English but immortality in Korean.

climax.text: Choosing words is often about choosing connotations—the emotional payload matters as much as the fact.

punchline.text: Same fact, different word, different feeling.

quiz.question: What is connotation?
options: The emotional or cultural associations of a word

hook.text: What separates 'boy' from 'girl'? Just one feature: [±female]. Everything else matches.

buildup.text: Semantic feature analysis breaks word meanings into bundles of binary features.

discovery.text: 'Bachelor' is [+human, +male, +adult, −married]—four features capture its meaning.

twist.text: The approach works well for some words but struggles with fuzzy categories like 'game' or 'art.'

climax.text: Feature analysis influenced AI's early attempts at representing word meaning computationally.

punchline.text: Words are bundles of features—some bundles are tidier than others.

quiz.question: What does semantic feature analysis do?

hook.text: 'Snow is white' is true if and only if snow is white. That sounds circular—but it's profound.

buildup.text: Truth-conditional semantics says a sentence's meaning is the conditions that make it true.

discovery.text: Alfred Tarski formalized this idea—it connects language directly to states of the world.

twist.text: Questions, commands, and exclamations don't seem to have truth values at all.

climax.text: Truth conditions work brilliantly for statements but leave much of language unexplained.

punchline.text: Meaning is what makes a sentence true or false.

quiz.question: What do truth conditions specify?
options: How many words a sentence has

hook.text: 'Bank' can mean a river bank or a financial bank—same word, two related origins.

buildup.text: Polysemy is when one word has multiple related meanings that branched from a common source.

discovery.text: 'Head' means body part, leader, top of a nail, and head of a table—all extended from one core.

twist.text: Polysemy differs from homonymy: 'bank' (river) and 'bank' (money) actually have separate origins.

climax.text: Most common English words are polysemous—the ten most frequent verbs average over 20 senses each.

punchline.text: The more common a word, the more meanings it carries.

quiz.question: What is polysemy?
options: One word with multiple related meanings

hook.text: 'Big' and 'large' seem interchangeable—but you say 'big sister,' never 'large sister.'

buildup.text: True synonyms—words interchangeable in every context—are almost nonexistent.

discovery.text: Synonyms differ in register, connotation, or collocation: 'purchase' vs 'buy,' 'commence' vs 'start.'

twist.text: Antonyms come in pairs: gradable (hot/cold), complementary (alive/dead), and converse (buy/sell).

climax.text: These semantic relations form networks that organize the entire mental dictionary.

punchline.text: No two words fit every slot the same way.

quiz.question: Why are true synonyms rare?
options: Words differ in connotation, register, or collocation
Synonyms are only found in poetry

hook.text: A robin is a bird. A bird is an animal. These 'is-a' links organize your mental dictionary.

buildup.text: 'Robin' is a hyponym of 'bird'; 'bird' is a hypernym of 'robin.'

discovery.text: Hyponymy creates a taxonomy—a tree of categories from specific to general.

twist.text: Speakers inherit properties down the tree: if birds have wings, robins have wings—no need to say it.

climax.text: This hierarchy powers AI knowledge bases and every library classification system.

punchline.text: Meaning flows downhill—from general to specific.

quiz.question: What is a hyponym?
options: A more specific term within a category

hook.text: 'Awful' once meant 'full of awe'—a compliment. Now it means terrible.

buildup.text: Word meanings drift over centuries through broadening, narrowing, and shifts in evaluation.

discovery.text: 'Meat' once meant any food; it narrowed to mean only animal flesh over time.

twist.text: 'Nice' started as 'ignorant' in Latin, drifted through 'foolish,' and ended up meaning 'pleasant.'

climax.text: Semantic change is constant—today's slang is tomorrow's standard vocabulary.

punchline.text: Words change their minds—slowly, but always.

hook.text: Is a penguin a bird? Technically yes—but it doesn't match your mental image of 'bird.'

buildup.text: Prototype theory says categories have best examples (prototypes) and fuzzier members.

discovery.text: Rosch showed that people rate robins as better birds than penguins—categories have internal structure.

twist.text: This challenges the classical view where membership is all-or-nothing based on features.

climax.text: Prototype effects appear everywhere: 'murder' is a more prototypical crime than 'jaywalking.'

punchline.text: Categories have centers and edges—not sharp lines.

quiz.question: What does prototype theory say about categories?
options: They have better and worse examples

hook.text: You've never heard 'the purple giraffe ate algebra' before—yet you understand it instantly.

buildup.text: The principle of compositionality says sentence meaning is built from word meanings plus structure.

discovery.text: Frege proposed this: know the parts and the rules, and you can compute any sentence's meaning.

twist.text: Idioms break compositionality—'kick the bucket' cannot be computed from its parts.

climax.text: Despite exceptions, compositionality explains how finite brains understand infinite sentences.

punchline.text: Meaning is parts plus rules—that's the recipe.

quiz.question: What is the principle of compositionality?
options: Sentence meaning comes from word meanings plus structure
Words have only one meaning each

hook.text: If 'John killed the spider,' then 'the spider is dead' must be true. No way around it.

buildup.text: Entailment is a meaning relation: sentence A entails sentence B if B must be true whenever A is.

discovery.text: Entailments are built into word meanings—'kill' entails 'die,' 'buy' entails 'pay.'

twist.text: Entailment is one-directional: the spider being dead doesn't entail that John killed it.

climax.text: Lawyers and logicians use entailment to test whether conclusions follow from premises.

punchline.text: Some truths ride on the back of others.

quiz.question: What does entailment mean?
options: If A is true, B must be true

hook.text: 'The king of France is bald.' Wait—France has no king. Is the sentence true, false, or neither?

buildup.text: Presuppositions are background assumptions a sentence takes for granted.

discovery.text: 'Stop smoking' presupposes you smoke; 'his car' presupposes he has one.

twist.text: Unlike entailments, presuppositions survive negation: 'He didn't stop smoking' still implies he smoked.

climax.text: Presupposition failure creates confusion—the listener's background assumption doesn't hold.

punchline.text: Half the meaning hides in what's already assumed.

quiz.question: How do presuppositions behave under negation?

hook.text: 'Every student read a book.' Did they all read the same book, or each a different one?

buildup.text: Quantifiers like 'every,' 'some,' and 'no' specify how many entities are involved.

discovery.text: Scope determines which quantifier takes precedence—different scopes yield different meanings.

twist.text: English word order doesn't always resolve scope—both readings are grammatically valid.

climax.text: Formal semantics uses logical notation to specify exactly which reading is intended.

punchline.text: The same words can count things two different ways.

hook.text: 'I ate' vs. 'I was eating'—both are past tense, but they frame the event differently.

buildup.text: Tense locates an event in time; aspect describes its internal structure—completed, ongoing, or repeated.

discovery.text: English marks aspect with auxiliaries: 'has eaten' (perfect) vs 'is eating' (progressive).

twist.text: Mandarin has no tense marking—particles like 'le' and 'zhe' mark aspect instead.

climax.text: Tense and aspect interact to create a rich timeline that sentences can zoom in or out of.

punchline.text: When it happened is tense; how it unfolded is aspect.

quiz.question: What does aspect describe?
options: The internal structure of an event

hook.text: 'Time is money.' You can't deposit time in a bank—yet the metaphor shapes how you think.

buildup.text: A metaphor maps structure from one domain (money) onto another (time).

discovery.text: Lakoff and Johnson showed that everyday language is saturated with metaphors we don't notice.

twist.text: 'Argument is war'—we 'attack' positions, 'defend' claims, and 'shoot down' ideas.

climax.text: Metaphors aren't decorations—they structure how we understand abstract concepts.

punchline.text: We think in metaphors more than we think about them.

quiz.question: What did Lakoff and Johnson show about metaphor?
options: Everyday language is saturated with metaphors

hook.text: 'The White House announced today...' A building can't talk—but you know exactly what it means.

buildup.text: Metonymy uses one entity to stand for a related one: container for contents, place for institution.

discovery.text: 'Lend me a hand' (hand for help), 'new blood' (blood for people)—metonymy is everywhere.

twist.text: Metonymy is not metaphor: metaphor maps across domains; metonymy stays within one domain.

climax.text: Both are cognitive shortcuts that compress complex ideas into compact expressions.

punchline.text: Name one thing and let it stand for another.

quiz.question: How does metonymy differ from metaphor?
options: Metonymy links related things in one domain

hook.text: It's pouring rain and you say 'Lovely weather!' Everyone laughs—the meaning is the opposite.

buildup.text: Verbal irony says one thing and means the reverse, relying on shared context.

discovery.text: Sarcasm adds a biting edge—it uses irony to mock or criticize.

twist.text: AI systems struggle with irony because the literal meaning is perfectly grammatical.

climax.text: Tone of voice is the main cue in speech; in text, emojis and punctuation sometimes help.

punchline.text: Say the opposite and trust the listener to flip it.

quiz.question: What defines verbal irony?
options: Saying one thing and meaning the opposite

hook.text: 'Spill the beans' has nothing to do with beans—it means to reveal a secret.

buildup.text: Idioms are fixed expressions whose meaning can't be predicted from their individual words.

discovery.text: They are stored in memory as whole units, like very long words with frozen structure.

twist.text: Some idioms are partially flexible—you can say 'the cat is out of the bag' in passive voice.

climax.text: Every language has idioms, and they rarely translate: French says 'tomber dans les pommes' for fainting.

punchline.text: Idioms break the rules—and every language has them.

quiz.question: Why can't idioms be translated word for word?
options: Their meaning doesn't come from individual words

hook.text: We say 'passed away' instead of 'died' and 'restroom' instead of 'toilet.'

buildup.text: Euphemisms are mild words that replace ones considered harsh, rude, or uncomfortable.

discovery.text: Taboo words trigger real physiological responses—increased heart rate and skin conductance.

twist.text: Euphemisms wear out: 'toilet' was itself a euphemism for an earlier term that felt too blunt.

climax.text: This 'euphemism treadmill' means every replacement eventually becomes the new taboo word.

punchline.text: We keep renaming the uncomfortable—it never stays polite.

hook.text: Russian has two mandatory words for blue—'siniy' (dark blue) and 'goluboy' (light blue).

buildup.text: Languages divide the color spectrum differently—some have only two or three basic color terms.

discovery.text: Berlin and Kay found a universal hierarchy: if a language has three terms, they're black, white, and red.

twist.text: Russian speakers distinguish blues faster than English speakers—language affects perception.

climax.text: Color naming sits at the intersection of biology, culture, and language.

punchline.text: The colors you name are the colors you see faster.

quiz.question: What did Berlin and Kay discover about color terms?
options: All languages have the same number

hook.text: English has one word for 'uncle.' Turkish has four—distinguishing mother's side from father's side.

buildup.text: Kinship terms vary wildly across languages, reflecting different family structures and social norms.

discovery.text: Hawaiian kinship uses the same term for mother and mother's sister—grouping by generation.

twist.text: These differences aren't just labels—they influence social obligations and family dynamics.

climax.text: Kinship systems show how deeply language and culture are intertwined in shaping meaning.

punchline.text: Who counts as 'family' depends on what your language calls them.

quiz.question: What does Hawaiian kinship terminology group by?

hook.text: You say 'the cup is on the table.' In Korean you'd specify whether the cup fits tightly or loosely.

buildup.text: Languages encode spatial relationships differently—English uses prepositions; Korean uses verbs.

discovery.text: Guugu Yimithirr speakers use compass directions instead of left and right—even indoors.

twist.text: These speakers have extraordinary spatial orientation—their language trains their navigation sense.

climax.text: Spatial language is a key test case for whether language shapes thought—and the evidence says yes.

punchline.text: How you describe space changes how you navigate it.

quiz.question: What do Guugu Yimithirr speakers use instead of left/right?

hook.text: Danish 'hygge,' Japanese 'wabi-sabi,' German 'Schadenfreude'—some words resist translation.

buildup.text: An untranslatable word packages a concept that another language takes a sentence to explain.

discovery.text: Portuguese 'saudade' captures a longing for something absent—no English word covers it exactly.

twist.text: Truly untranslatable words are rare—the concept can always be explained, just not in one word.

climax.text: These words reveal cultural priorities: what a society cares about, it names concisely.

punchline.text: What a culture values, its language names in one word.

quiz.question: What does 'saudade' in Portuguese express?
options: A deep longing for something absent

hook.text: Every language has words for 'water,' 'eat,' 'die,' and 'big.' Some meanings are universal.

buildup.text: Anna Wierzbicka proposed about 65 semantic primitives found in every human language.

discovery.text: These include 'I,' 'you,' 'someone,' 'something,' 'want,' 'know,' 'good,' 'bad.'

twist.text: Complex concepts can be defined using only these primitives—a universal metalanguage.

climax.text: If true, it means beneath surface diversity, human languages share a common semantic core.

punchline.text: Deep down, all languages mean the same basics.

quiz.question: What are semantic primitives?
options: Basic meanings found in all languages

hook.text: You know about 50,000 words—and can retrieve any one in less than 200 milliseconds.

buildup.text: The mental lexicon is your brain's dictionary—organized not alphabetically but by meaning and sound.

discovery.text: Words are linked by meaning (dog→cat), sound (dog→log), and association (dog→bone).

twist.text: The tip-of-the-tongue state proves the lexicon is real—you know the word exists but can't find it.

climax.text: Priming studies show that hearing 'doctor' speeds up recognition of 'nurse.'

punchline.text: Your brain's dictionary has no alphabet—just connections.

quiz.question: How is the mental lexicon organized?
options: By meaning and sound networks, not alphabetically

hook.text: Say 'salt' and most people instantly respond 'pepper.' The link is automatic.

buildup.text: Word association tests reveal how concepts are linked in the mental lexicon.

discovery.text: Adults tend to give syntagmatic responses (salt→pepper); children give paradigmatic ones (salt→sugar).

twist.text: This shift happens around age seven and reflects the growing organization of semantic networks.

climax.text: Association patterns are remarkably consistent across speakers of the same language.

punchline.text: Your word links reveal how your mind maps the world.

quiz.question: What response do adults typically give in word association?

hook.text: Hear 'bread' and you'll recognize 'butter' faster than 'nurse.' Your brain pre-activated it.

buildup.text: Semantic priming occurs when one word speeds up processing of a related word.

discovery.text: Meyer and Schvaneveldt demonstrated this in 1971 using reaction-time experiments.

twist.text: Priming is automatic and unconscious—it happens even when you don't notice the prime word.

climax.text: This reveals that the brain doesn't access words in isolation—it activates whole neighborhoods.

punchline.text: One word wakes up its neighbors before you even ask.

quiz.question: What does semantic priming demonstrate?
options: Related words activate each other in the brain
Only visual words prime each other

hook.text: We say 'the future lies ahead' and 'the past is behind us.' We think of time as a path.

buildup.text: Conceptual metaphor theory says abstract thinking is grounded in physical experience.

discovery.text: We understand 'more is up' (prices rise), 'affection is warmth' (warm feelings), and 'ideas are objects.'

twist.text: Aymara speakers gesture behind for the future—their time metaphor is reversed.

climax.text: These metaphors aren't universals—they vary across cultures and languages.

punchline.text: We understand the abstract through the concrete.

quiz.question: What does conceptual metaphor theory claim?
options: Abstract thought is grounded in physical experience

topics.title: Meaning in the Age of AI

hook.text: Large language models produce fluent text—but do they understand what their words mean?

buildup.text: LLMs learn word associations from vast data without ever experiencing the real world.

discovery.text: They capture distributional meaning—words that appear in similar contexts have similar vectors.

twist.text: Critics argue this is pattern matching, not understanding—no grounding in actual experience.

climax.text: The debate echoes centuries of philosophical arguments about what 'meaning' really requires.

punchline.text: Machines process meaning—whether they have it is the open question.

quiz.question: What kind of meaning do LLMs capture?
